title: School Kitchen Garden — Chapter Summary
intro: A kitchen garden is a small useful garden where you grow plants you can eat. This chapter teaches you to plan, plant and care for one at school. You will learn the right spot, the right season, the simple tools, the steps from seed to harvest, and how to share what you grow. A kitchen garden teaches planning, observation, patience and teamwork — and gives you fresh food in return.

sections.heading: What a Kitchen Garden Is
bullets: A small garden that grows plants you can eat — vegetables, herbs, sometimes fruits.
Different from a flower garden (beauty) and a forest (wild).
Can be five pots or a school plot — the principle is the same.
Plants need soil, water, sunlight, air and care.
Benefits: fresh food, learning, pollinators, greener school, friendships.

sections.heading: Planning the Garden
bullets: Pick a spot with at least 4–6 hours of sunlight.
Stay away from heavy footfall and close to a water source.
Three Indian seasons: Kharif (Jun–Sep), Rabi (Oct–Mar), Zaid (Mar–Jun).
Easy first crops: spinach, coriander, tomato, lady's finger, mint, chilli.
Sketch a plan: tall plants behind, leave a hand's-width between herbs.

sections.heading: Tools and Materials
bullets: Khurpi — small hand-hoe for digging and weeding.
Trowel — for transplanting seedlings.
Watering can — for gentle watering.
Soil + compost in a 2:1 ratio.
Mulch (dry leaves), stakes, gloves, wooden tags.
Always wash hands with soap after gardening.

sections.heading: Sowing and Growing
bullets: Three ways to start a plant: direct sowing, seedlings, cuttings.
Direct sowing: spinach, coriander, radish.
Seedlings: tomato, brinjal, chilli.
Cuttings: mint, curry leaves.
Seeds need moisture, warmth and time.
Drop seeds, cover lightly with soil, water gently, label the row.

sections.heading: Caring for Plants
bullets: Water early morning or late afternoon — not at noon.
Touch the soil before watering: if moist, skip a day.
Weed once a week; pull out by the roots.
Mulch keeps soil moist and weed-free.
Pests: pick caterpillars off, spray mild neem-water, plant marigolds.
Stake tall plants (tomato, brinjal); keep a garden diary.

sections.heading: Harvesting and Reflection
bullets: Spinach / coriander — pick large outer leaves; plant keeps growing.
Radish / carrot — pull up when the root is firm.
Tomato / brinjal / chilli — pluck when ripe.
Wash, share with the school cook, take some home with permission.
Save seeds from your best plants for next season.
Reflect: what thrived? what struggled? what would I do differently?

key_takeaways: A kitchen garden grows plants you can eat; needs sun, soil, water, air and care.
Plan a sunny spot, pick the season (Kharif / Rabi / Zaid), sketch a layout.
Use simple tools — khurpi, trowel, watering can — and work safely.
Start plants by direct sowing, seedlings or cuttings.
Care daily: water mornings, weed weekly, mulch, watch for pests, stake tall plants.
Harvest carefully; wash, share, and save seeds from the best plants.
Keep a garden diary — reflection turns experience into skill.

glossary.definition: A small garden used to grow plants for food — vegetables, herbs, sometimes fruits.
The Indian growing season for crops sown in June/July with the monsoon and harvested by autumn.
The Indian winter growing season — crops are sown in October/November and harvested in February/March.
A short Indian summer growing season — crops are sown in March/April.
A small hand-held hoe used for digging and weeding in a small garden.
A small hand tool with a scoop, used to transplant seedlings.
Decomposed organic matter (kitchen waste, leaves) added to soil for nutrients.
A layer of dry leaves, hay or coconut fibre placed on the soil to keep it moist and weed-free.
Placing seeds straight into the bed where they will grow, with no transplanting.
A young plant raised in a tray, later transplanted into the main bed.
A piece of stem of a plant placed in moist soil so that it grows roots and becomes a new plant.
The process by which a seed sprouts and starts to grow into a plant.
An unwanted plant that takes water, nutrients and light away from your crops.
A small animal or insect (e.g. caterpillar, aphid) that damages plants.
A simple notebook in which you record dates, weather, observations and actions in your garden.
